topics.mechanism_2026-10-11: Parent discussed set 3 #34 (PP+QQ=RST, 'what digit does R represent', answer A=1) with her directly. Her gap: she doesn't spontaneously think to BOUND the problem -- i.e. reason 'PP and QQ are each at most 99 and 88 (different repeated digits), so the sum can't exceed 187, which is under 200, so R must be 1.' This bounding-the-extremes strategy is the standard approach for 'what digit must this be' cryptarithm questions and she doesn't reach for it on her own yet. Real strategy gap, worth walking through explicitly as a named technique ('when a digit question asks what MUST be true, try bounding the max/min first') rather than just re-explaining this one problem.
topics.parent_flagged_ambiguity_2026-10-11: Parent raised a concern that the question wording ('what digit does R represent') isn't deterministic without the real original's 'PP and QQ need to be as large as possible' constraint, since R could in principle be 0. Checked this carefully: it does NOT hold up -- the question explicitly states 'each letter represents a different digit from 1 through 9,' which excludes 0 as a possible value for ANY letter including R, by the problem's own stated domain. Separately, since PP+QQ maxes out at 187 and must be >=100 for the sum to display as a 3-digit RST at all, R is forced to be 1 for every valid assignment (not just the 'largest possible' one) -- confirmed by construction with a concrete valid solution (P=8,Q=5,R=1,S=4,T=3: 88+55=143, all 5 digits distinct, none zero). The 'as large as possible' phrase in the real original problem was likely needed to pin down a UNIQUE value of S or T (which DO vary across valid P,Q choices), not R, which is invariant. So this problem's phrasing is fine as published -- no live-worksheet fix made. Documenting the reasoning here in case it needs revisiting.

topics.mechanism_2026-10-11: CONFIRMED (parent watched her work #21 directly, 9/15 shaded): her default fraction-to-percent method is 'find x so that denominator x x = 100, then numerator x x' -- i.e. scale the ORIGINAL denominator straight to 100. This only produces a clean answer when the denominator is already a factor of 100 (2,4,5,10,20,25,50...). 15 is not (100/15 isn't a whole number), so the method breaks down and she mis-converts (landed on 90% instead of 60%). She has two reliable fallbacks available but doesn't default to either: (1) simplify the fraction FIRST, then scale -- 9/15 -> 3/5, and 5 IS a factor of 100 (x20), giving 3x20=60% cleanly; (2) direct long division, 9÷15=0.6=60%, which always works regardless of the denominator. This is the actual mechanism behind the existing 'decimal-vs-nonnice-fraction' habit tag (flagged in set 2 but never written up with a cause) -- not a concept gap (she understands fraction=percent equivalence fine), a PROCEDURE gap: no reliable fallback when the quick mental shortcut doesn't land on a whole number.

This matches the EXISTING 'off-by-10' habit already tracked under 'Multi-step unit conversion (off-by-10, multi-step)' (confirmed set 2 #32, originally from an Elevate Prep drill) -- same cross-topic zero-miscounting pattern, new context, not a new issue. Not a fraction-conversion concept gap. Parent taught a general verification technique: to check if a decimal equals a candidate fraction, multiply the decimal by the denominator and see if it lands on the numerator (e.g. 0.045 x 200 = 9, confirms C; 0.045 x 20 = 0.9, not 9, rules out A) -- a good general cross-check that catches zero-count slips a surface eyeball comparison misses.
